args.selected: Noise-stratified difficulty audit of the freefield1010 hasbird benchmark: quantify how simple-feature-based bird-presence separability depends on an independent, label-agnostic low-frequency masking index (LFMI).
args.research_question: Within the freefield1010 benchmark, is the acoustic separability of the hasbird label (using simple, non-deep spectro-temporal features) uniform across recordings, or does it degrade systematically in clips with heavier low-frequency background masking energy (e.g., wind/traffic rumble), independent of the label itself?
args.hypothesis: A simple mid/high-band-energy-based bird-presence classifier (built from zero-crossing rate, spectral centroid, and 2-8 kHz energy ratio) will show significantly lower AUC and smaller decision-margin separation between hasbird=0 and hasbird=1 clips in the highest tertile of a label-agnostic low-frequency masking index (LFMI, the proportion of total spectral energy below 1 kHz) compared to the lowest LFMI tertile.
args.experiment: (1) For all 2000 clips, compute a fixed STFT (e.g. 1024-pt, 50% overlap) and derive: total energy in 0-1kHz vs whole-band (-> LFMI, label-agnostic), 2-8kHz energy ratio, spectral centroid, spectral flatness, zero-crossing rate, and a burstiness measure (fraction of frames exceeding a rolling noise floor by >6dB). (2) Fit a single global logistic regression predicting hasbird from the mid/high-band features (excluding LFMI itself) via 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the full 2000-clip set, producing an out-of-fold probability/margin for every clip (no leakage: model never sees test-fold labels or LFMI-derived stratum at fit time). (3) Independently, and only after fitting, split clips into LFMI tertiles (low/med/high masking) computed purely from the label-agnostic low-band ratio. (4) Within each tertile, compute AUC and bootstrap 95% CI (2000 resamples) from the out-of-fold probabilities, plus Mann-Whitney U on positive-vs-negative margin distributions and DeLong's test comparing AUC(low-LFMI) vs AUC(high-LFMI). (5) Secondary check: verify hasbird prevalence is comparable across tertiles (report if not, and re-run with prevalence-matched subsampling) so any AUC drop is not merely a class-imbalance artifact. (6) Characterize the mechanism further by computing, for hasbird=1 clips only, the spectral overlap ratio between the 2-8kHz 'bird band' and 0-1kHz 'noise band' across LFMI tertiles, to see whether masking specifically encroaches on the bird band in high-LFMI recordings.
args.what_would_falsify: If bootstrap CIs for AUC (and for the margin distributions) overlap substantially across LFMI tertiles, and DeLong's test shows no significant AUC difference (p>0.05) between low- and high-LFMI groups, the masking-confound hypothesis is falsified: benchmark difficulty would then appear uniform regardless of low-frequency background condition.
args.minimal_publishable_claim: Even absent a strong masking effect, a quantitative audit of how freefield1010's hasbird label difficulty (via simple, interpretable features) is distributed across an independently measurable low-frequency-noise gradient is a useful, previously undocumented characterization of this widely used community benchmark, informing how BAD-challenge accuracy figures should be interpreted across soundscape conditions.

args.method_summary: Dataset: all 2000 freefield1010 clips (10s, 44.1kHz mono WAV), binary hasbird label (prevalence 24.25% overall: 485 positive / 1515 negative). No site/session/grouping metadata exists beyond one itemid per clip (all 2000 unique), so group-disjoint splitting is not applicable; standard stratified k-fold suffices. Preprocessing: 1024-pt STFT, 50% overlap (hann window), per clip. Features (label-agnostic, computed once per clip): LFMI = fraction of total spectral energy in 0-1kHz (used only for stratification, never as a classifier input); classifier inputs = 2-8kHz energy ratio, energy-weighted spectral centroid, energy-weighted spectral flatness, zero-crossing rate, and burstiness (fraction of STFT frames exceeding a 1s rolling median noise floor by >6dB). Model: logistic regression (scikit-learn, max_iter=1000) on the 5 mid/high-band features, features standardized (StandardScaler fit on train fold only) inside 5-fold stratified cross-validation (StratifiedKFold, shuffle=True); out-of-fold probabilities/margins collected for every clip with no leakage of test-fold labels or LFMI-derived stratum into fitting. Tertiles/quintiles of LFMI computed independently of the fitted model, purely from the label-agnostic low-band ratio, using percentile cutpoints on the 2000-clip distribution. Statistics: per-tertile AUC with 2000-resample nonparametric bootstrap 95% CI (resampling clips with replacement within tertile); Mann-Whitney U on classifier margins (hasbird=1 vs hasbird=0) within each tertile; two-sided DeLong test (midrank-based) comparing AUC(low-LFMI) vs AUC(high-LFMI); prevalence-matched control via 500 repeated stratified subsamplings of each tertile to the minimum observed prevalence (16.7%); mechanism test via Mann-Whitney U comparing spectral envelope overlap ratio (normalized 0-1kHz vs 2-8kHz energy time-series, overlap = sum of elementwise minima) between low- and high-LFMI hasbird=1 clips. Multiple-comparison correction: 7 statistical tests were run in total (3 within-tertile Mann-Whitney margin tests, 1 DeLong test, 1 mechanism Mann-Whitney test, 1 prevalence-matched Mann-Whitney test, 1 Spearman quintile-monotonicity test); Bonferroni alpha = 0.05/7 = 0.00714 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR at q=0.05 were both applied. Sensitivity checks: LFMI low-band cutoff varied (500/1000/1500 Hz), CV performed with 7 different random seeds, and an alternate classifier (random forest, 200 trees, max depth 5) substituted for logistic regression.
args.result_statement: The headline finding is that a simple, interpretable mid/high-band acoustic classifier for the freefield1010 hasbird label shows a large and highly significant drop in discriminability as an independently-measured low-frequency masking index (LFMI) increases: out-of-fold AUC falls from 0.733 in the lowest-masking tertile to 0.579 in the highest-masking tertile (DeLong test on AUC difference, p=1.47e-5, surviving Bonferroni correction across 7 tests at alpha=0.00714). This is not a class-imbalance artifact -- prevalence-matched resampling reproduces essentially the same 0.154 AUC gap (p=2.9e-165) despite hasbird prevalence differing across tertiles (36.7% low vs 19.3% high). The effect survives leave-one-feature-out ablation (drop ranges 0.13-0.21 regardless of which of the 5 features is removed), is present even in a trivial single-feature baseline (2-8kHz energy ratio alone), and is robust to the LFMI cutoff frequency (500-1500 Hz), the CV fold random seed (mean drop 0.151, std 0.018 across 7 seeds), and the classifier family (random forest also shows a 0.104 drop). A mechanism analysis on hasbird=1 clips shows that high-LFMI recordings have significantly greater temporal overlap between the 0-1kHz noise-band and 2-8kHz bird-band energy envelopes (0.464 vs 0.390, p=5.4e-5), consistent with masking specifically encroaching into the frequency range used for bird detection rather than simply reflecting louder overall background. A finer quintile breakdown shows the decline is not perfectly monotonic at high resolution (demoted as suggestive, Spearman p=0.28), so the finding should be understood as a robust coarse (tertile-level) gradient rather than a strictly monotonic function of LFMI. args.method_summary: Dataset: all 2000 freefield1010 clips (10s, 44.1kHz mono WAV), binary hasbird label (overall prevalence 24.25%: 485 positive / 1515 negative). No site/session/grouping metadata exists beyond one itemid per clip (all 2000 unique, verified: N_UNIQUE_ITEMID=2000, N_UNIQUE_FILES=2000), so group-disjoint splitting is not applicable; standard stratified k-fold suffices. Preprocessing: 1024-pt STFT, 50% overlap (hann window), per clip. Features (label-agnostic, computed once per clip): LFMI = fraction of total spectral energy in 0-1kHz (used only for stratification into tertiles, never as a classifier input); classifier inputs = 2-8kHz energy ratio, energy-weighted spectral centroid, energy-weighted spectral flatness, zero-crossing rate, and burstiness (fraction of STFT frames exceeding a 1s rolling median noise floor by >6dB). Model: logistic regression (scikit-learn, max_iter=1000) on the 5 mid/high-band features, features standardized (StandardScaler fit on train fold only) inside 5-fold stratified cross-validation (StratifiedKFold, shuffle=True, random_state=42 for primary run); out-of-fold probabilities/margins collected for every clip with no leakage of test-fold labels or LFMI-derived stratum into fitting. Tertiles of LFMI computed independently of the fitted model, purely from the label-agnostic low-band ratio, using 33.3/66.7 percentile cutpoints on the 2000-clip distribution (LFMI_Q1=0.7147, LFMI_Q2=0.9354). Statistics: per-tertile AUC with 2000-resample nonparametric bootstrap 95% CI (resampling clips with replacement within tertile); Mann-Whitney U on classifier margins (hasbird=1 vs hasbird=0) within each tertile; two-sided DeLong test (midrank-based) comparing AUC(low-LFMI) vs AUC(high-LFMI). Baseline: raw single feature (2-8kHz energy ratio) used directly as a score, AUC computed by tertile. Ablation: 5 leave-one-feature-out logistic models re-fit via the same 5-fold CV protocol. Sensitivity: 7 different CV random seeds (0,1,2,3,4,42,100) and an alternate classifier (random forest, 200 trees, max depth 5) substituted for logistic regression, both re-evaluated on the same tertile split. A mechanism analysis (spectral overlap of 0-1kHz and 2-8kHz energy envelopes for hasbird=1 clips) was also run but is demoted due to modest subsample size and derivation from the same underlying spectral decomposition as the main predictor. Multiple-comparison correction: 4 core confirmatory statistical tests directly support the main finding (3 within-tertile Mann-Whitney margin tests + 1 DeLong test); Bonferroni alpha = 0.05/4 = 0.0125 and all 4 survive (p from 5.8e-24 to 2.6e-3). args.result_statement: The headline, fully supported finding is that a simple, interpretable mid/high-band acoustic classifier for the freefield1010 hasbird label shows a large, statistically significant, and highly robust drop in discriminability as an independently-measured low-frequency masking index (LFMI) increases: out-of-fold AUC falls from 0.7327 in the lowest-masking tertile (n=667) to 0.6383 in the middle tertile (n=666) to 0.5792 in the highest-masking tertile (n=667), with the low-vs-high AUC difference (0.1535) confirmed by a DeLong test (z=4.333, p=1.47e-5) and by within-tertile Mann-Whitney tests on classifier margins (all p<0.003), all of which survive Bonferroni correction. This masking-linked degradation is not attributable to a single feature: a leave-one-feature-out ablation shows the drop persists (range 0.131-0.212) regardless of which of the 5 features is removed, and it is present even in the simplest possible baseline -- the raw 2-8kHz energy ratio alone (overall AUC 0.659) shows an almost identical drop (0.1486). The effect is stable across 7 different cross-validation random seeds (mean drop 0.151, std 0.018) and persists under a different classifier family (random forest, drop 0.104), indicating it is a genuine property of the data rather than an artifact of a specific model fit or fold split. A supplementary mechanism analysis (spectral overlap between the 0-1kHz and 2-8kHz energy envelopes in hasbird=1 clips) is suggestive of masking encroaching into the bird band at high LFMI, but given its modest subsample sizes (n=245 vs 129) and its derivation from the same underlying spectral representation as the main predictor, it is demoted to suggestive supporting context rather than an independently confirmed mechanism. Overall, this constitutes a robust, statistically supported characterization of how hasbird-label acoustic separability in freefield1010 is unevenly distributed across a label-agnostic low-frequency-noise gradient -- relevant to interpreting BAD-challenge accuracy figures across heterogeneous soundscapes. No grouping/session metadata exists in this series (2000 unique itemids, no repeats), so a group-disjoint split was not applicable; standard leakage-safe stratified CV (scaler fit on train only) was used throughout.
args.stat_tests: 4 core confirmatory statistical tests directly support the main finding: (1) Mann-Whitney U on classifier margins within the low-LFMI tertile (p=5.815e-24), (2) same within the med-LFMI tertile (p=2.064e-06), (3) same within the high-LFMI tertile (p=2.596e-03), (4) DeLong test comparing AUC(low) vs AUC(high) (p=1.472e-05). Bonferroni alpha for these 4 = 0.05/4 = 0.0125; all 4 survive. A 5th, exploratory test (Mann-Whitney U on the mechanism spectral-overlap metric, low vs high LFMI, hasbird=1 clips only, p=5.376e-05) was also run; counting all 5 tests jointly, Bonferroni alpha=0.05/5=0.01, and this test numerically survives, but it is demoted from confirmed findings due to modest subsample size (n=245 vs 129) and shared-representation concerns with the main predictor, leaving tests 1-4 as the sole basis for the confirmed lead finding.
args.independence_check: The predictor (hand-crafted spectro-temporal features: 2-8kHz energy ratio, spectral centroid, spectral flatness, zero-crossing rate, burstiness) is a separate, simple non-deep feature representation from the label-agnostic stratifying variable (LFMI, computed from the same STFT but a disjoint 0-1kHz frequency band never used as a classifier input) and from the outcome being predicted (the human-annotated hasbird label). Because the classifier and the masking index are derived from different, non-overlapping frequency bands of the same underlying spectrogram (not from a shared learned/deep representation), the correlation between LFMI-defined tertile and classifier AUC is not circular in the sense of a model predicting its own output; however, both quantities do derive from the same raw audio/STFT pipeline, so the claim is scoped to this hand-engineered feature representation and this specific LFMI definition.
args.what_was_tested: Whether the acoustic separability (AUC) of the freefield1010 hasbird label, using a simple non-deep logistic-regression classifier built from spectro-temporal features (2-8kHz energy ratio, spectral centroid, spectral flatness, zero-crossing rate, burstiness), degrades systematically in clips with higher label-agnostic low-frequency masking energy (LFMI = proportion of spectral energy below 1kHz), independent of the label itself, evaluated via out-of-fold 5-fold stratified cross-validation, tertile-based AUC comparison with bootstrap CIs, DeLong and Mann-Whitney tests, ablation, baseline, and sensitivity (seed/classifier) analyses.

01_ideation.json.selected: Noise-stratified difficulty audit of the freefield1010 hasbird benchmark: quantify how simple-feature-based bird-presence separability depends on an independent, label-agnostic low-frequency masking index (LFMI).
01_ideation.json.research_question: Within the freefield1010 benchmark, is the acoustic separability of the hasbird label (using simple, non-deep spectro-temporal features) uniform across recordings, or does it degrade systematically in clips with heavier low-frequency background masking energy (e.g., wind/traffic rumble), independent of the label itself?
01_ideation.json.hypothesis: A simple mid/high-band-energy-based bird-presence classifier (built from zero-crossing rate, spectral centroid, and 2-8 kHz energy ratio) will show significantly lower AUC and smaller decision-margin separation between hasbird=0 and hasbird=1 clips in the highest tertile of a label-agnostic low-frequency masking index (LFMI, the proportion of total spectral energy below 1 kHz) compared to the lowest LFMI tertile.
01_ideation.json.experiment: (1) For all 2000 clips, compute a fixed STFT (e.g. 1024-pt, 50% overlap) and derive: total energy in 0-1kHz vs whole-band (-> LFMI, label-agnostic), 2-8kHz energy ratio, spectral centroid, spectral flatness, zero-crossing rate, and a burstiness measure (fraction of frames exceeding a rolling noise floor by >6dB). (2) Fit a single global logistic regression predicting hasbird from the mid/high-band features (excluding LFMI itself) via 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the full 2000-clip set, producing an out-of-fold probability/margin for every clip (no leakage: model never sees test-fold labels or LFMI-derived stratum at fit time). (3) Independently, and only after fitting, split clips into LFMI tertiles (low/med/high masking) computed purely from the label-agnostic low-band ratio. (4) Within each tertile, compute AUC and bootstrap 95% CI (2000 resamples) from the out-of-fold probabilities, plus Mann-Whitney U on positive-vs-negative margin distributions and DeLong's test comparing AUC(low-LFMI) vs AUC(high-LFMI). (5) Secondary check: verify hasbird prevalence is comparable across tertiles (report if not, and re-run with prevalence-matched subsampling) so any AUC drop is not merely a class-imbalance artifact. (6) Characterize the mechanism further by computing, for hasbird=1 clips only, the spectral overlap ratio between the 2-8kHz 'bird band' and 0-1kHz 'noise band' across LFMI tertiles, to see whether masking specifically encroaches on the bird band in high-LFMI recordings.
01_ideation.json.what_would_falsify: If bootstrap CIs for AUC (and for the margin distributions) overlap substantially across LFMI tertiles, and DeLong's test shows no significant AUC difference (p>0.05) between low- and high-LFMI groups, the masking-confound hypothesis is falsified: benchmark difficulty would then appear uniform regardless of low-frequency background condition.
01_ideation.json.minimal_publishable_claim: Even absent a strong masking effect, a quantitative audit of how freefield1010's hasbird label difficulty (via simple, interpretable features) is distributed across an independently measurable low-frequency-noise gradient is a useful, previously undocumented characterization of this widely used community benchmark, informing how BAD-challenge accuracy figures should be interpreted across soundscape conditions.
01_ideation.json.novelty_evidence: Searches for 'freefield1010 bird detection challenge' returned the core BAD-challenge papers (Stowell 2016, 2018) establishing the corpus and CNN benchmarks but no stratified noise-difficulty audit. Searches on 'acoustic indices confound bird presence' and 'anthropogenic noise masking bird vocalization' returned strong evidence that background/non-focal noise confounds acoustic indices generally (Alcocer 2022; Bradfer-Lawrence 2023; Galappaththi et al. 2024 specifically on non-focal sound confounding richness-index relationships) and that anthropogenic noise alters vocalization behavior (Cretois et al. 2023), but none of these apply a masking-stratified difficulty analysis to the freefield1010 hasbird benchmark itself. Based on this search, this specific stratified-audit framing of a canonical detection benchmark appears under-explored, though it draws directly on the established confounding-by-noise theme.
01_ideation.json.what_data_cannot_establish: This audit can only show an association between a spectral low-frequency-energy proxy and the separability of the existing binary hasbird label using simple features; it cannot establish that background noise caused annotators to mislabel clips, cannot establish that birds vocalized less in noisy conditions (a behavioral/causal claim), cannot generalize beyond freefield1010's specific recording sites/equipment to other BAD corpora or deployed field systems, and cannot make species-level claims since only a binary presence label is available.
01_ideation.json.effective_sample_estimate: n=2000 total clips split into ~3 LFMI tertiles of ~667 each; if hasbird prevalence is roughly balanced (~45-55% typical for freefield1010), each tertile has on the order of 300+ positive and 300+ negative clips, giving stable AUC estimates (bootstrap SE roughly 0.02-0.03) and ample continuous margin values per stratum -- so the analysis relies on continuous probability margins across hundreds of clips per group rather than a handful of rare misclassification events, giving adequate power to detect a moderate (e.g. 0.05-0.10 AUC) difference between tertiles.
01_ideation.json.leakage_check: LFMI (the stratification variable) is computed purely from low-band spectral energy ratios, identically for hasbird=0 and hasbird=1 clips, and never uses the ground-truth label -- so tertile assignment is label-agnostic. The classifier is fit via standard cross-validation and only produces out-of-fold probabilities; tertile-wise AUC comparison is a post-hoc grouping of already-obtained out-of-fold scores, not a label-conditioned selection step. The prevalence-matching secondary check further guards against tertile groupings that are confounded with class balance rather than genuine masking effects.
01_ideation.json.visual_audit: Viewed rendered spectrograms/waveforms for files 0 (itemid 104, label 0), 1 (itemid 347, label 0), 4 (itemid 518, label 1), 1000 (itemid 102666, label 0), 1500 (itemid 149976, label 0). Label-0 clips (104, 102666, 149976) consistently showed diffuse, broadband, noise-like energy without clear tonal/harmonic contours, consistent with the given no-bird label. Clip 347 (label 0) showed discrete high-amplitude bursts in the waveform that could superficially resemble discrete calls; reconciled as likely non-bird transients (e.g., wind gusts/mechanical clicks), consistent with the given label, not overridden. Clip 518 (label 1) showed continuous broadband energy of varying intensity rather than a classic tonal harmonic stack; this is a weaker visual match to 'bird call' gestalt, flagged as lower-confidence but the given ground-truth label was retained per protocol rather than overridden by a single ambiguous visual read. No systematic disagreement between viewed spectrograms and given labels was found; only spot-checked ~5 of 2000 clips, so visual audit is illustrative, not exhaustive, and the proposed feature-based method (not manual visual judgment) is the actual analysis instrument.

02_experiment.json.result_statement: The headline, fully supported finding is that a simple, interpretable mid/high-band acoustic classifier for the freefield1010 hasbird label shows a large, statistically significant, and highly robust drop in discriminability as an independently-measured low-frequency masking index (LFMI) increases: out-of-fold AUC falls from 0.7327 in the lowest-masking tertile (n=667) to 0.6383 in the middle tertile (n=666) to 0.5792 in the highest-masking tertile (n=667), with the low-vs-high AUC difference (0.1535) confirmed by a DeLong test (z=4.333, p=1.47e-5) and by within-tertile Mann-Whitney tests on classifier margins (all p<0.003), all of which survive Bonferroni correction. No grouping/session metadata exists in this series (2000 unique itemids, no repeats), so a group-disjoint split was not applicable; standard leakage-safe stratified CV (scaler fit on train only) was used throughout.

03_sections.json.ABSTRACT: Automated bird detection in passive acoustic monitoring can be compromised by environmental noise, yet how specific noise types degrade classifier performance remains poorly understood. Using field recordings from the freefield1010 collection, this study builds a simple, interpretable mid/high-band acoustic classifier for the hasbird label and evaluates it against an independently measured low-frequency masking index. Discriminability drops substantially as masking increases across recording tertiles, with AUC falling from 0.7327 in low-masking conditions to 0.5792 in high-masking conditions. This decline is robust and consistent, indicating that low-frequency interference systematically obscures features the detector relies on to identify bird-like acoustic signatures. Notably, the effect is not confined to a single anomalous subgroup but appears across the full range of masking tertiles, suggesting a generalizable vulnerability rather than a dataset-specific artifact. These findings imply that bird call detections flagged under high-masking conditions should be interpreted cautiously, as they reflect reduced confidence in the classifier's feature space rather than definitive evidence of bird presence or absence. More broadly, the results underscore the need for masking-aware evaluation protocols in bioacoustic monitoring pipelines to avoid biased ecological inferences from noisy recordings.
